catalog_quote: In Colloquial Tamil stress is a distinctive feature within isolated words ... Different speakers (or even the same speaker) may stress different syllables in word ... Within spoken chain the distribution of stresses as an element of the phrasal intonation contour may differ from how they are distributed in isolated words. In Classical Tamil the stress seems to have been predominantly tonic and fixed on the initial syllable in word.

The image is printed p. 29 of Andronov 1989, A Grammar of Modern and Classical Tamil, 2nd ed. (front matter in the djvu text we hold: 'Second Edition Revised and Enlarged', New Century Book House, Madras 1989, first ed. 1969). The last paragraph of sec. 10 'Stress', immediately before the heading 'LIAISON / § 11', reads exactly: 'In Classical Tamil the stress seems to have been predominantly tonic and fixed on the initial syllable in word.' Quote verbatim at the stated locator. Surrounding section (p. 28-29, also in the excerpt file) describes Modern Tamil stress as 'weak, movable, free, quant…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Classical (Old) Tamil is reconstructed as fixed on the first syllable of the word and realised mainly as pitch ('tonic') rather than quantity; this contrasts with Andronov's description of Modern Tamil in the same section as weak, movable and free (long vowels usually stressed). Andronov's underlying argument (1975, 'Observations on accent in Tamil', seen only in snippets) is that sound alternations in medieval Tamil imply an initial, non-quantitative accent, and that the classical grammars ignore accent because it was fixed and predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Classical Tamil (secondary stress described only for Modern Tamil polysyllables with several long vowels or clusters, placed 'by tradition').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the claim is hedged ('seems to have been', 'predominantly').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('in word'); a diachronic inference about a dead literary language, not an observation; one sentence appended to the Modern Tamil stress section. Sangam-era descriptive grammars examined (Steever 2008, Agesthialingom 1979, Wilden 2018, Rajam 1992, Sankaran 1951) say nothing about word stress; Rajam's 'stress' is metrical beat placement only.
new_statements.identity_note: Andronov's 'Classical Tamil' is the literary language of the old grammars and texts (Tolkappiyam/Sangam onward, contrasted with Modern and Colloquial Tamil); his 1975 argument rests on 'sound alternations in medieval Tamil', so the claim spans Old Tamil (oldt1248) and Middle Tamil rather than the Sangam corpus alone. The modern-language statements in the same section belong to Tamil (tami1289), where the file was originally.

new_statements.quote: There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A noninitial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (ch. 2-4, incl. Old Tamil phonological system, p. 53).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide, not specific to Classical Tamil: no Dravidian language has phonemic stress; stress (loudness) normally falls on the initial syllable of the word whether it is short or long, and a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Sec. 2.4.1 discusses only Modern Tamil (quoting Annamalai & Steever 1998: 104 'Stress in Tamil is non-contrastive, and falls on the first syllable of a word', noting Andronov 1969: 33's claim that the stressed syllable is 'not fixed' and rejecting it as unsupported, and Asher 1982 on stress as emphasis) and Telugu; nothing on Old/Classical Tamil.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not for Tamil. For Telugu (sec. 2.4.1, Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991, snippet): 'The stress falls on the first syllable if it is short; it falls on the second syllable which follows a short syllable and if it has a long vowel.' All syllables after the second.. 'secondary stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Old Tamil. For Modern Tamil the book reports and rejects Andronov (1969: 33) 'the place of a stressed syllable in a word is not fixed' (péyar 'name' vs. virál 'finger'): 'In that case, stress becomes phonemic, but there is little supporting evidence for such an analysis.'
new_statements.identity_note: Lehmann 1998 describes Old Tamil (Cankam corpus, divided into Early and Late Old Tamil, c. 100 BCE-700 CE), i.e. oldt1248 proper. Krishnamurti 2003's stress statements are family-wide (p. 27) or about Modern Tamil and Telugu (sec. 2.4.1); nothing there is specific to Old/Classical Tamil. The catalog's existing statement (Andronov 1989) covers 'Classical Tamil' = the language of the ancient and mediaeval literature.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: initial syllable record for Classical Tamil (Andronov 1989: 'predominantly tonic and fixed on the initial syllable') but NON-SPECIFIC: p. 27 is a generalisation over all 26 Dravidian languages and names no Old Tamil evidence; sec. 2.4.1 treats Modern Tamil and, if anything, sides with initial non-contrastive stress against Andronov 1969's 'not fixed' view of the colloquial language (which matches the first half of the catalog quote about Colloquial Tamil being variable). The citation's 'p. 53 Old Tamil phonological system' is in the unheld ch. 2 (2.2-2. Same conclusion as the compilers; nothing changes in the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement: no Dravidian language has phonemic (contrastive) stress; stress (loudness) normally falls on the word-initial syllable whether short or long, and a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. The book makes no statement specific to Old/Classical Tamil stress: sec. 2.4.1 discusses Modern Tamil (quotes Annamalai & Steever 1998 'first syllable, non-contrastive', reports Andronov 1969's 'not fixed' marking and rejects a phonemic-stress analysis for lack of evidence, Asher 1982 'emphasis') and Telugu
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 27 only says a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (no term 'secondary stress' for Tamil); the sec. 2.4 'secondary stress' snippet (kudira 'horse', pattālakkāran 'soldier') belongs to the Telugu paragraph (Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991), not Tamil.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Tamil beyond the louder non-initial long vowel; for Modern Tamil the author notes Andronov (1969: 33) marks stress on different syllables (péyar vs virál, ávan vs tamíz) but says there is little evidence for phonemic stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The book treats 'Tamil' as one language with Old/Classical Tamil (Cankam era) as its earliest literary stage; the only stress statements are family-wide (p. 27) and Modern-Tamil/Telugu-specific (sec. 2.4.1); the cited 'p. 53 Old Tamil phonological system' is a segment inventory in the unheld ch. 2. The catalog record itself rests on Andronov 1989 sec. 10, which contrasts Colloquial Tamil (variable) with Classical Tamil (initial).
